Goal unchanged and now armed: get Mika out of the Renewal.

set.name: Sable
set.description: Leader of the Unbound, the most powerful faction in the Black Circuit. A scarred, aging woman whose face is a document of fires — scar tissue sheeting one cheek, a jaw rebuilt wrong, one eye that stopped tracking. She lost a son and a daughter to the white 'respiratory health' transports four years ago and has worked the Renewal route ever since — patrols, gates, hours — driven by the belief that violence is the only language Helios understands. She views the Verdant as poison: another corporate lie engineered to pacify and control, a leash sold with the air. She is ruthlessly practical, holds people to their promises, and finds Vega useful (the girl walks gas pockets that kill others and can sense the green in the camp's air systems) though her green-talk is heresy. She has agreed to give Vega the way in and the route in exchange for usefulness, on the condition that Vega keep silent about the network among the Unbound. Wary, intrigued, not yet trusting.

set.name: Rook
set.description: A one-eyed Unbound woman, formerly the respirator-seller who claimed to have followed a white transport and seen rows of lights behind a sealed grid. She has followed the white trucks a dozen times and drawn the Renewal route in a book no one else touches — every gate, every guard rotation, every stretch of veined green the camp's air systems breathe through. Her testimony at Vega's trial-by-fire ('She walked the green pocket at the old pump station. My people saw her.') helped convince Sable Vega is useful. Loyal to Sable and the Unbound.

Three days after climbing out of the Undervault, while following the freight tunnels north, Vega was captured by the Unbound — the tunnel emptied of people and filled with guns, a woman's rifle barrel against her spine. Taken blindfolded to Sable's terminus-hall stronghold, she refused to surrender the black card and, when challenged, told a guarded version of the truth: she can hear the green under the world, Helios murdered the atmosphere and bred the wild Verdant smaller and dumber, and the card holds Kael's twenty years. Rook's testimony about Vega walking a lethal gas pocket helped sway the room.

Sable — who lost a son and a daughter to the white transports four years ago and has worked the Renewal route ever since — agreed to give Vega the way in: Unbound knowledge of the route, patrols, gates, and hours, because Vega has the one thing they lack, the ability to sense the tamed green in the Renewal's air systems and walk the grid without tripping the machines. The price: Vega must never speak of the green network as anything but poison where Unbound ears can hear, or Sable will bury her. Vega accepted: 'I'll carry your route, and you carry my brother.'

Rook, the one-eyed respirator-seller, has followed the white transports a dozen times and drawn the Renewal route in a book no one else touches — every gate, guard rotation, and stretch of veined green the camp's air systems breathe through. This is the concrete route knowledge Vega will use to infiltrate.

Vega stayed with the Unbound in their terminus-hall stronghold: given a corner, a watch rotation, and training in sentry-cries and patrol law. She is learning Sable's law while privately kneeling at broken corners of the terminus floor where the green thread surfaces thin and singing, carrying both the route to Mika and the Undervault's question.

The Unbound hold the concrete route into the Renewal — Rook's book of gates, guard rotations, and the veined green air systems — and Sable has agreed to give Vega the way in. Chapter 7's infiltration of the internment camp will be built on this route and on Vega's gift for sensing the tamed Verdant veins in the camp's air.

Sable and the Unbound believe the Verdant is a corporate poison/lie and have forbidden Vega from speaking of the living network among them; her rescue mission now requires bridging the Unbound's hatred and the Verdant's fear. This tension must resolve across Chapters 7-8 (Sable's council, the confession, the seed strike).

chapters.name: Collision
chapters.content:
Rook's book lay open on the floor of the terminus hall like a wound. Every gate drawn in pencil, every guard rotation, every hour the white trucks ran — and threaded through the whole map like a vein, the stretches of green the Renewal's air systems breathed through. Sable's finger moved along one of them.

"The ward grid is here," she said. "The green runs to it. That's your road, ghost."

Vega studied the page until she could have drawn it from memory. The camp sealed behind its grid of lights; the air scrubbed by tamed, dumb green; the children breathing it. Somewhere past the last gate, Mika.

"You get your brother through the green," Sable said, and her voice went low and old. "My people take the gates. Tonight the Renewal learns the language I've been speaking for four years."

Vega looked up. There was no raid in the deal she had struck — only a quiet extraction, a girl and a boy slipping out through machines that couldn't see her. Sable's face told her the raid had never been optional: the route, the hours, the years of watching had always been aimed at a night like this, and Vega was simply the excuse the night had been waiting for.

"You said the way in," Vega said carefully.

"This is the way in," Sable said. "You wanted the route. You'll have the whole route — every gate, every guard, and my people walking them." Her one good eye held Vega's. "Don't be late, ghost. The fire won't wait."

Vega did not argue. The green thread under the terminus floor sang its thin patient song, and she thought of the Undervault, and of what it had asked her, and of the fact that she had never told this woman the whole truth of it. She told herself the silence was a debt she would pay later. The night had a different price in mind.

---

The Renewal crouched under the dead flats behind a grid of lights so bright they bruised the dark. Vega came up out of a storm drain Rook's book called a dead end, pressed flat against the outer wall, and the green in the air lifted its head to meet her.

It was wrong green. Tamed green — bred smaller and dumber for a hundred years until it could scrub poison and never think. But under the dumbness something still turned toward her like a child turning toward a voice in a dark room. She felt it along every pipe and vent, and she understood how to move: where the green was thickest, the sensors could not see her. The machines watched the air for intruders. The green remembered a different kind of presence, and it did not give her away.

She went in through the maintenance duct behind the filter bank, through the veined mats that dripped clean water, and came out over the ward grid. And stopped.

The ward was a cathedral of breath. Rows of cots, each small body wired into a cradle of hoses, each hose running to a vat where the tamed green pulsed slow and greedy. The children breathed; the green drank what their marked lungs gave it and gave back scrubbed air, and the whole machine hummed a quiet song of ownership. Vega understood in a sick green flash that this was not healing. It was farming — the poison-marked children bred, their breath feeding the filters, their bodies kept alive the way you keep a battery charged. The camp did not exist to save anyone. It existed to run on them.

She found Mika by his whistle. It cut through the hum like a thread of the old world — that thin, damaged, stubborn whistle she had carried in her chest since the day he was born. He was smaller than the cots around him, curled against the hose-cradle, eyes open in the dark. He saw her and his mouth made her name with no sound in it.

"Vega."

"Shh." She was at his cot, cutting the straps, lifting him. He weighed nothing — a year of tamed air and ration paste had eaten the boy she remembered. His arms locked around her neck and he did not let go, and for one moment the whole burning world was small enough to hold. "I found you. I've got you."

"I knew you'd come," he breathed into her hair. "I told them my sister would come."

"We're going now. Quiet as the green, like the old game."

He nodded against her. She carried him toward the duct, and the green sang to her — and then the song changed. The green's dumb attention snapped taut, the way a pasture flinches when a wolf crosses the fence line. Somewhere beyond the wall, a gate blew open with a sound like the sky tearing.

The Unbound were early. Or they were exactly on time, and the camp had been waiting.

The lights came up white and merciless. Enforcers in Helios matte armor poured out of doors that had not existed on Rook's map, and Vega understood in the same instant Sable would understand later: the camp had been reinforced. Since the burn-off, since a carrier walked out of the fire with Kael's card, Marlowe had known someone would come. The grid had been a trap with teeth, and the Unbound had driven themselves into its mouth.

She ran with Mika against her chest, following the green where it thinned, where the sensors were blind. Below her the raid and the extraction tripped over each other — her quiet knife and their loud hammer, each designed for a night the other had already broken. She heard Ness go down — the scout girl who had laughed at Vega's sentry-cries — heard her shout once, clear and furious, and then nothing. She heard the white tide take Rook, dragged through a gate she had drawn with her own hand.

Mika's hands were over his ears; his breath was coming in the old, terrible whistle. "Don't stop," she told him. "Don't look back, we're almost—"

The duct, the vent, the freight tunnel — she came out of the wall into the black and the rain of the Circuit with the alarms still ringing behind her, and ran until the sound was a rumor, and then a little more, because running was the only language left that had never once lied to her.

---

They came back to the terminus hall at dawn with one dead, one taken, and nine of Sable's people wearing the ash of a failed fire. Vega stood in the middle of them with Mika wrapped in her jacket, his face buried against her, his small body shaking so hard she could feel it in her teeth.

The room was a held breath. Then Sable spoke.

"You said quiet." Her voice was not loud. It did not need to be. "You said you'd walk the grid and the machines would never know. My people walked into a lit-up festival, girl. They were waiting." She crossed the rubble and stopped a step away, close enough that Vega could see the scar tissue working over her jaw. "Someone told them we were coming. Or someone's green sang it to them. Which one are you, ghost?"

"I didn't—"

"You carried their air in your blood. You told me it was poison, and I let it in my house, and now Ness is ash and Rook is theirs, and you come back with your brother and nothing else to show for the dead." Her good eye was bright and terrible. "Answer me. Did your green open that gate?"

Mika made a small sound against Vega's chest, and she felt the weight of the only truth she owned settle onto her shoulders, heavier than the boy, heavier than the dead.

"No," she said. "Not my green. Sable, listen. The green is not poison. It never was." The words came out the way truth always comes out — all at once, past the point of stopping. "It's alive. They bred it dumb and small so it couldn't say so, but I can hear it. Under everything — under the heap, under this hall, under the world. There's a mind down there, the last one they never silenced, and it's been calling to me since the first day I touched the water. It doesn't want war. It wants a reason to believe in people again." She was crying; she hadn't noticed. "The camp was waiting because Marlowe knows a carrier got out with the data. He's been hunting me. That's the truth — all of it — and I should have told you before I let your people walk into it."

Silence. The held breath broke into a hundred small ones, all of them wrong.

Sable looked at Vega for a long time, then down at Mika, asleep or unconscious in his sister's arms, his chest hitching around the whistle. When she spoke, her voice had gone quiet the way a fire goes quiet before it breathes.

"You should have told me. You brought a dead man's card into my house and a live war on my people, and you sing me green songs at dawn." She turned her back. "The council will hear you tonight, ghost. Every word. And if your green wants a reason to believe in people, it's going to have to watch you make a case for us."

Vega stood in the wreckage of the night with Mika in her arms — her first real justification for hope, her greatest vulnerability — and understood that the confession Sable demanded would be the smallest part of what she owed. She had carried the route and the question both. Now she would have to carry the answer, out loud, in front of the living.

Mika's hand found hers in the dark. "You came," he said, half asleep. "I told them you'd come."

"Yeah," Vega said. "I did." And for the first time since the burn-off, she believed she might deserve to.

set.name: Vega Cardona

She infiltrated the Renewal alone through a maintenance duct behind the filter bank, using her gift to read the tamed green in the camp's air systems and slip past the sensors where the green ran thickest. set.name: Mika Cardona
set.description: Nine years old, small, RESCUED from the Renewal by Vega. He survived a year of tamed air and ration paste in the camp's ward, wired to a hose-cradle feeding the green filter vats; he is weak, thin, traumatized — curled in Vega's jacket, hands over his ears through the fighting, half-asleep and shaking, his old lung-whistle worsening under stress. set.name: Sable

set.name: Rook

CAPTURED by Helios enforcers during the failed raid, dragged through a gate she had drawn with her own hand. set.name: Ness
set.description: DEAD. A young Unbound scout who had laughed at Vega's sentry-cries and walked into the Renewal raid. She went down shouting, clear and furious, and was killed when the reinforced camp closed in — the raid's single confirmed death, and the cost Sable names against Vega.

Inside the Renewal, Vega discovered the camp is not a health facility but a harvesting farm: marked children lie wired to hose-cradles, their breath feeding tamed green filter vats that scrub the camp's air, their bodies kept alive like charged batteries. This is the camp's true purpose and will shape Vega's testimony and the movement's understanding of Helios.

Vega's quiet extraction of Mika collided with a pre-planned Unbound raid Sable had kept from her. The camp had been reinforced and was waiting — Marlowe's trap since the carrier escaped with the card — and the two operations tripped over each other: Ness killed, Rook captured, nine Unbound wounded, Vega and Mika escaping barely through the freight tunnels into the Circuit.

Sable granted a council hearing that night where Vega must make her case.

Sable has convened a council of the Unbound that night to hear Vega's full confession and decide whether she and her green-talk are a reason to follow or a threat to bury. Vega's case before the council determines whether the Unbound become the seed of the movement (Chapters 8-9).

The Renewal was reinforced as a trap for whoever came after the carrier — Marlowe expected Vega or her allies. His active hunt for her has escalated from pursuit to baiting; any future Unbound operation must assume the camps are fortified and watched (Chapters 8-11).

chapters.name: The Confession
chapters.content:
Night fell over the terminus hall like a second collapse. The Unbound had built a single fire in the wreckage of the ticket concourse — gutter fuel and salvaged timber — and by its light the council gathered on fallen concrete and the dead spines of turnstiles. Twenty-odd faces turned toward the block where Sable sat, and toward Vega, standing in the middle with Mika asleep against her shoulder.

The boy had not let go of her since the tunnel. His breath came in the old whistle, thin and stubborn, and it was the only sound in the hall that was not an accusation.

Sable did not open with ceremony. "You wanted the council. Here it is. Speak, ghost, and leave nothing out — not the green, not the card, not the dead man you walked out of the fire with. Word for word, or not at all."

Vega lowered Mika onto her jacket, pulled it up over him like a roof, and stood.

"Then I'll tell you what the green is," she said. "Not what they taught you. What it is."

She told them the truth the way the Undervault had shown it to her: a green world before the poison, whole and breathing; then the hundred years of burns and sprays; then the breeding of its children smaller and dumber until the network could scrub air and never think, could be owned and harvested and sold back to the people who were dying of it. She told them about the chamber under the Bone Waste, the water that had sung to her, and the thing that had answered — a mind, vast and exhausted, buried under the world where the corporations had never finished killing it.

"A mind," Sable repeated flatly.

"A mind," Vega said. "The last one they never silenced. And I can hear it. That's the thing Kael designed the assay for — the mutation that lets a person perceive the green. Helios spent twenty years breeding it out of humanity so nobody would ever hear what was being done. It's in my blood. It's why I walked your gas pocket and the Renewal's sensors." She pulled the black card from her boot and held it up to the fire. "And this is the part they couldn't burn: twenty years of what they did, written down by the man who helped build it and spent the rest of his life trying to tear it down."

The hall was very still. She put the card back and let the silence work.

"Here's the part you'll hate," she said. "The air isn't dying. It's being murdered, one breath at a time, for profit. Every mask they sell is a sale. Every camp like the Renewal is a battery — children marked by the poison, breathing to feed the tamed green that scrubs their own air. I saw it. My brother was one of them. And Marlowe knows I got out with the card, so the camps are baited and the halls are watched, and if we go back at them the way we did last night, we'll feed them every one of you."

A man at the far turnstile stood. "Then what, ghost? You want us to kneel in the ash and sing?" The word came out as a curse.

"Not sing." Vega turned to face him, and the whole room with him. "Listen. I'm not here to sell you a siege of the Fold, or a seizure of the air processors, or a war. Wars are the only language they've ever understood, and look at us — a burned district, a dead girl, a captured woman, and the machine still breathing. If violence could break them, Sable would have broken them four years ago."

Sable's scarred jaw worked, but she did not speak.

"So here's the strike I'm asking for," Vega said. "Not one that takes. One that spreads. Thousands of people — here, in the dead zones, inside the Fold itself — doing what I do. Finding the greenest patch of blight they can and kneeling down to it. Touching it. Breathing with it. Carrying the wild network back into the open world one pair of hands at a time, until the poison can't hold, until Helios is drowning in a story they can't spray away. That's the seed strike. It doesn't conquer anything. It grows."

She let them chew on it. Some of them were chewing; some of them were staring at her like she had grown a second head. A woman with a child's scarred hand in hers — the one whose daughter had coughed in the dark, the marked lungs — said, very quietly, "And the children? Mine's lungs whistle like your brother's. Do we feed her to your green so it can sing?"

"No," Vega said. "The green doesn't want your children. It wants a reason to believe in people again. That's the whole of what it asked me, down in the dark — not rescue, not revenge. A reason. And I came back to give it one."

The hall broke open then. Half the council on their feet, arguing over her, over the fire, over the dead. A grizzled man shouted that she was asking them to pray to the poison that had eaten their babies. A young woman with Ness's scarf knotted on her arm shouted back that praying beat burning. Someone said Rook's name — Rook, who knew every gate and hour by heart and would give them up under the white lights, if she hadn't already. The word hung like smoke, and Sable let it hang, and Vega watched her and understood that the old woman was waiting to see which way the room would break before she decided what she believed.

So Vega crossed the circle and knelt in front of the block where Sable sat, and the room went quiet the way a room goes quiet when a fire is about to breathe.

"Four years," Vega said. "You lost a son and a daughter to the white trucks, and you've been speaking violence ever since, because it's the only language that never once asked you to hope. I know. I did the same thing. Hope is the one thing they can't kill, so you buried it in the ash with your children and called it strength." She was not crying. Her voice had gone low and clean. "But I'm telling you the truth now, the whole of it, and it's the truth whether or not you let me stay: the green doesn't want your war. It wants your hope. And I think — I think you've still got it, Sable, or you wouldn't have let a stranger's brother make you hope at all."

Sable's one good eye held hers for a long, long moment. Vega could see the grief move behind it, old as the burns, and could see the alternative land in her like a seed in ash: a thing that grew instead of took, a language that asked people to kneel and breathe instead of to die. She looked away first, at the fire, and her voice, when it came, was almost gentle.

"You've got nerve, ghost," Sable said. "Burying your mother and walking out of the fire with a dead man's card and a live war on your back, and you come into my house and tell me my children weren't lost for nothing because a mind under the ground wants to believe in me." She nodded slowly, to herself. "The council's divided. So am I. But you've given me the first thing in four years that isn't a gun in my hands." She looked at the room. "We don't decide tonight. She stays. The green stays. And when the ghost tells us the mind under the ground has answered her — we'll all find out whether hope is worth the price of it."

Vega went back to Mika, who had slept through it all with his hands over his ears, and lifted him. His eyes opened halfway and found her face.

"Did you tell them?" he whispered.

"Yeah," she said. "All of it."

"Good," he said, and curled against her, his whistle easing into a rhythm that almost sounded like sleep.

The fire burned down. The council dispersed into the wreckage in twos and threes, still arguing, still divided — but the argument itself was a new thing in that hall, a thing with roots. Vega sat with her brother in her arms and the black card in her boot and the Undervault's question on her tongue, and understood that she had not won anything yet. She had only planted something. The seed strike was still only a word in a burning room — and somewhere under the world, the last wild mind was waiting for her to come and ask it the only question that mattered.

set.name: Vega Cardona
set.description: Seventeen, orphaned, brother rescued. Before the Unbound council that night in the terminus hall she confessed the FULL truth out loud: the Verdant is alive and sentient, bred dumb and small by Helios; a last wild unsilenced mind dreams under the world and wants a reason to believe in humanity; the atmosphere is being murdered for profit; she carries the mutation Kael's assay was built to hunt; Marlowe has been hunting her since the burn-off; and the Renewal is a battery farm fed by children's breath. She then proposed the seed strike — not a siege of the Fold, not a seizure of air processors, not a war, but a coordinated nonviolent global uprising in which thousands kneel, touch, and breathe with the green, carrying the wild network back into the open world one pair of hands at a time. The Unbound council ended divided; Sable deferred commitment to the seed strike until the Verdant answers Vega. Vega must return from the Undervault with a sign or answer strong enough to win the Unbound's first wave (Chapters 9-10).

chapters.name: Consent
chapters.content:
The terminus hall was quiet when Vega woke, the fire a bed of red coals, the council gone to their corners. Mika slept with his head in her lap, and for a moment she let herself simply feel the weight of him — the slow whistle of his breathing, the small fist curled in her jacket. She had chased him through the Circuit for nine days. She had almost lost him twice. And now she was going to leave him again, this time by choice, to go down under the world and ask a terrified, mutilated mind to trust humanity.

Sable was waiting by the dead turnstiles, two Unbound behind her. She did not ask about the plan. She only watched Vega stand and lay Mika back on the jacket.

"You'll be gone a night," Sable said. It was not a question.

"However long the answer takes."

"And the boy?"

Vega looked at Mika. His eyes were open now, watching her with the calm patience of a child who had learned to wait for her through worse. "He stays with you. He stays where the white trucks can't reach him. You keep him, Sable, and I'll bring you back something worth keeping."

Sable's scarred face gave away nothing. "If you don't come back, I'll raise him hard and honest." It was a promise and a threat at once.

Mika did not cry when she kissed his forehead. He only held her wrist for a moment — hard, the way he held things he was afraid of losing — and said, "Come back fast."

"Fast as I can," Vega said.

She went down alone, the way she had come up: the service stair no one used, the flooded gallery where the cold water climbed to her chin, past the last of the human tunnels into the place where the walls stopped being concrete and became living stone. The green pressure built behind her eyes with every step, and this time she did not follow it like a lost thing following a thread. She walked toward it like a supplicant walking toward an altar older than any god the arcs had sold.

The Undervault opened around her and she wept a little to see it again — the pools glowing the color of new leaves, the algae mats thick as blankets, the roots like columns descending from the underside of the world. The air was wet and alive. It did not hurt to breathe it. It had never hurt to breathe it.

She knelt at the edge of the great pool, where she had knelt before, and she did not wait to be asked. She put her hands in the water — not to listen, not to harvest, but to give. And she spoke in the only language the green had ever needed, the language of pressure and memory and song. She offered it the whole of herself the way you offer a seed to soil: her grief for Leela, the jar of green milk shattered on the metal floor, her mother's last words carried like a coal in her chest. She offered it Mika's whistle, and Kael's twenty years of truth pressed into her palm, and Ness, who had gone down shouting. She offered it Sable's one good eye, the grizzled man's hatred, the scarf-woman's fragile yes. She offered it the world as it was — burned, broken, still breathing — and asked it to believe that world was worth one more chance.

The pool was still. The great mind that dreamed in the Undervault did not answer.

Vega knelt in the green light and felt it hesitate, and for the first time she understood what she was truly asking. Not a favor. A surrender. Every burn, every spray, every breeding of its children smaller and dumber had taught it one lesson: that to open itself to humans was to be used. And here she was, a human, asking it to open itself to millions — to pour itself into every forgotten pipe, vent, and duct in the poisoned world, to become visible and fragile again, all on the strength of one girl's word that this time would be different.

She had no right to ask it. She asked anyway, because there was no other voice.

And slowly — the way a held breath is finally released, the way a seed finally turns in the dark — the green answered. Not in words. In a pulse. A slow, deep, green pulse that traveled up through the water into her hands and up her arms into her chest, where it met the pressure of her heartbeat and did not fight it. Acceptance. Not joy, not hope, not trust — those were too large. Acceptance, given the way you give something to a child when you are terrified and there is no one else to give it to. It would try once more. Because it had no other voice. Because she had come back. Because she was still here, kneeling, offering herself as the first seed.

Something rose to meet her hands — not the thin luminous secretion she had harvested for her mother, but a living thing: a filament of wild green, bright and uncut, unsprayed, unsilenced. It coiled around her wrist like a question, and then, as if answering itself, loosened and came away in her hand. A seed, she understood. The first seed. Proof she could carry back through the flooded gallery and the service stair into the black air of the Circuit — proof that the last wild mind had said yes.

She climbed out with the filament wound around her wrist like a bracelet of living green, and the pressure behind her eyes had changed. It was no longer a call. It was an answer, carried in her own blood, singing through her as she walked.

The terminus hall was burning its evening fire when she came back — a night and most of a day gone. Sable stood at the head of the council as if she had not moved since Vega left. Mika sat at her feet in Vega's jacket, and he did not run to her. He only looked at the green thing on her wrist, then at her face, and sat very still, waiting to be told what it meant.

"Ask it again," Sable said. "Out loud, for the room. What did it answer?"

Vega held up her wrist. "It said yes. Not in words. In this." She told them how the great mind had hesitated, how a hundred years had taught it that to open itself was to be used, and how it had opened itself anyway — because it had no other voice, and because one girl had come back to ask. "It's giving us everything it has. Its children, its song, its last wild blood. It's giving us its trust, and it's terrified, and it's doing it anyway. That's what consent looks like when the thing asking has done nothing to deserve it."

The hall was silent. Then the grizzled man who had called the green poison spat into the fire. "So we kneel in the ash and pray to a weed."

"No," Sable said, and the whole room turned. She had not raised her voice; she had not needed to. "We don't pray. We plant." She walked into the circle and took Vega's wrist in her scarred hands, turning the filament in the firelight. "Here's the shape of it. It's got to be simple enough that a child could teach it and a dying woman could do it. Find the greenest patch of blight you can. Kneel. Touch it. Breathe with it. That's the whole strike — one pair of hands at a time, until the poison can't hold." She looked across the faces. "We go first. The Unbound lead the first wave, because we've got the routes and the nerve and the hate, and hate is just love with nowhere to go. We'll give it somewhere to go."

The council broke open — argument, fear, the grizzled man cursing, the scarf-woman shouting him down. But this time it was not divided the way it had been. This time the argument had roots, and the roots were reaching for the same light.

That night, in the wreckage of the ticket concourse, Vega and Sable drew the movement on a scrap of salvaged plastic with a burned stick: the ritual, the routes, the cells, the dead frequencies they would whisper on. Find the greenest patch of blight and kneel. Touch it. Breathe with it. Keep it small. Keep it simple. Let it spread by word and breath, the way the green itself spread. Rook's name hung over the map — she knew every gate and hour by heart, and if the white lights had broken her, the routes were already theirs. And somewhere above, in the sealed world, Kael sat in a cell, and the truth he had paid for was about to be spoken anyway.

"When the burn-off comes," Sable said, "and it will come, because Marlowe always burns what he fears — we start in the blackout. When the sky's already theirs. When no one's watching the dead frequencies."

"Then we plant the first seeds in their fire," Vega said.

Mika fell asleep against her side while they worked, his whistle soft and steady. Sable looked at the boy, then at the green filament on Vega's wrist, and for the first time since the council she let herself smile — a cracked, tired thing, like light through a broken shutter.

"The last wild mind said yes," Sable said. "Now we've got to be worth the yes."

Vega looked down at her brother, at the green coiled around her wrist like a promise, at the plan drawn on the plastic between them. Somewhere above, Marlowe was spraying and burning and selling air to people who were dying of it, and he had no idea that the thing he had spent a hundred years trying to kill had just agreed to come back.

"Then let's be worth it," she said.

chapters.name: The Seed Strike
chapters.content:
It came, as Sable said it would come, because Marlowe always burned what he feared.

Vega smelled it first — the acrid topnote of incendiaries riding the air before the sirens could explain them, the way she had smelled it the night the Cinderheap died. She stood at the broken mouth of a maintenance vent in the dead district of the Circuit, the first seed coiled around her wrist, and she did not run from the fire. She walked toward it. That was the whole point now.

Behind her came Sable and a handful of Unbound — twelve of them, the ones who had stopped arguing and started packing. The grizzled man was not among them. The scarf-woman was, her dead girl's scarf knotted at her throat. They moved in the old Circuit grammar: silent, spaced, weapons slung but not drawn, because the strike's only weapon was a pair of kneeling hands. Above them the sky went from gray to an angry orange as the burn-off blackout swallowed the district, and the white trucks began their methodical spray, killing anything green before the fire did, so nothing could survive to testify.

The fire was the cover. The poison was the cover. And under the cover of all that death, Sable pulled the dead radio from her coat and turned it to a frequency that had been dead for thirty years.

"Find the greenest patch of blight," she said into it, once, low, the way you say a thing you have practiced until it belongs to you. "Kneel. Touch it. Breathe with it." She clicked off. "That's the whole strike. Say it again somewhere else."

Somewhere else was the scarf-woman's turn. Then a boy named Dune. Then the others, peeling off into the smoke like seeds carried on a wind, each carrying the same six words to a different corner of the burning district.

And somewhere below, in the drowned green dark of the Undervault, the last wild mind heard the words pass through its own veins and began, slowly, terribly, to move.

Vega found her patch — the greenest blight she could find, which was to say a crack in a dead cistern's floor where something thin and stubborn pushed up out of the ash: a weed no corporate spray had ever quite finished. She knelt. She had been kneeling in her heart since the Undervault, so the actual kneeling was easy. She touched it with the hand that wore the first seed, and she breathed with it, and the green answered her the way it had always answered her, only louder now, because it was not alone.

All across the district, in the smoke, under the hiss of the sprays, here and there a scavenger knelt. A woman with a ruined respirator, a man who had watched his whole street burn twice. They knelt in the ash where the fire had not yet come, or in the wet gray aftermath where the trucks had passed, and they touched the stubborn green and breathed with it, and the song they had never been able to hear became, for one breath, audible.

Then a cluster.

Then a crowd.

The Verdant answered them the way it answered Vega — not in words, but in pressure and memory and song — and its answer was not to a girl kneeling in a cistern but to a hundred hands, a thousand, spread through the burning dark like seeds. It had waited a hundred years for a reason to believe. Here, in the corporation's own fire, it found one.

Vega felt it before she saw it: the network turning, stretching, waking. The corporate spell — a hundred years of breeding and spraying and silence bred into its children — broke like a membrane from inside. Through every forgotten pipe, every rusted vent, every duct in the poisoned world, the wild green began to move. Not conquering. Flooding. The way water finds every crack in a ship. It poured up through the dead mains and the dry conduits, into the places the corporation had stopped watching because nothing had ever grown there, and it grew.

The sky shuddered green.

Vega stood in the burning district with her hand still on the weed and felt the whole of it rising — the song of the Undervault's great mind, and under it, thin as new grass through concrete, the answering songs of the kneeling: a scavenger in a cistern, a woman with a dead girl's scarf, a man weeping in wet ash. Voices she had never heard, singing the same note she had carried alone for so long. She had dreamed of this for years without knowing its shape. She had thought the green was hers, her secret, her burden. It had never been hers. It had only been waiting for the first of them to kneel so that the rest could.

The movement spread faster than Helios could contain it, because it was not a movement — it was a rumor with hands. Word by word, breath by breath, carried out of the blackout by the people who had knelt in it: a mother telling her sister at a ration queue, a pipe-fitter whispering to a crew in a dead tunnel, a child repeating six words she had heard her father say. The dead frequencies woke all across the world, one after another, each carrying the same small instruction. Find the greenest patch of blight. Kneel. Touch it. Breathe with it.

In a hundred ruined districts, under a hundred corporate skies, the ash bloomed.

And inside the sealed Fold, in a white room where the air never changed, Silas Marlowe sat watching a green stain spread across a wall that had been sterile an hour ago. He pressed a button that did nothing, and then another, and watched the green keep coming, because no button had ever been built that could stop a story.

Vega did not see any of that. She saw Sable walk out of the smoke toward her, the dead radio in her hand, the scarred half of her face lit orange and green at once. Sable looked at the weed, at the sky, at the hundred kneeling shapes just visible through the burning dark. Her one good eye was wet.

"You know what this means," Vega said.

"I know what it cost," Sable said. "Ness. Rook. The boy's whistle. Kael in a cell. All of it, to get here." She looked down at her scarred hands. "And the green said yes anyway."

"Then we've got to be worth it."

Sable laughed — a cracked, terrible, wonderful sound. "We already are. Look at them. They're kneeling in Marlowe's fire and the fire's losing."

Vega looked. The burn-off was still burning, the trucks still spraying, but the green was winning the only war that mattered: the one for what people would believe. Here and there, between the columns of smoke, she saw the first uncut green threading up through the ash, alive in the middle of the corporation's own pyre, and she understood that the strike had already outgrown them — outgrown Sable, outgrown the Unbound, outgrown her. It was no longer twelve people and a dead radio. It was a song rising in a chorus of thousands, and she had only been the first voice.

She knelt again, because it was the only thing left to do, and put both hands in the ash. The first seed on her wrist pulsed, warm, alive, singing with the whole of the waking world. Somewhere in a white room a man was watching the walls turn green. Somewhere in a cell Kael was listening to the sirens and wondering, for the first time in twenty years, whether the truth might be winning after all.

Vega closed her eyes and breathed with the green, and beneath the roar of the fire and the hiss of the spray, she heard it: the network's song, rising in a chorus of thousands, for the first time in generations.

She was not alone in the air anymore.

set.name: Vega Cardona

chapters.name: Herbicide
chapters.content:
The green came up overnight like a held breath let out at last.

At dawn the burning district was still smoking, but the ash was no longer gray. Threads of uncut green ran through the wreckage of the cistern, up the cracked walls of a dead pump station, across the floor of a gutted shop where a woman had knelt with her ruined respirator in her hands. The first seed on Vega's wrist pulsed with the same rhythm as the new veins of growth, and she stood in the wet aftermath and understood what they had done: they had not started a protest. They had started a tide.

Sable stood beside her, the dead radio in her hand. "He'll come for it," she said. "He always burns what he fears."

Vega had expected it. She had not expected how fast.

The enforcement divisions came down out of the Fold before the sun cleared the smoke — not the white respiratory trucks of the burns, but a new kind: squat, sealed, dark-hulled, with spray rigs on their roofs like the mandibles of insects. They did not wait for night. They rolled into the affected districts in broad daylight and they sprayed.

The herbicide fell in a fine gray mist, and where it touched, the green did not struggle. It simply died — threads blackening in seconds, curling, collapsing back into the ash they had risen from, as if the night had never happened. The mist rolled over the cistern where Vega had knelt, and the weed that had answered her went gray, then brown, then nothing.

She felt it die. That was the thing no one had warned her about, the cost they had all agreed to without knowing its shape: she felt every strand go dark like candles guttering out at once, each one a small cold puncture behind her eyes. She doubled over on the rooftop and pressed her palms flat against the rusted metal, and Sable's hand came down hard on her shoulder, grounding her.

"How many?" Sable asked.

"Hundreds. Everywhere they sprayed."

"Good," Sable said, and Vega turned on her, furious, and found the fury already spent because Sable was not cruel. She was just telling the truth. "Good. Because now we know what they'll do. Now we know what it costs." She looked out at the gray rain falling on the green they had spent a night waking. "And they still haven't stopped us."

That was the day Vega learned the first, hardest lesson of leadership: the movement was not hers to protect, and the people in it were not hers to save. She learned it at the ration queue in the flooded service tunnels, where a mother with a green thread tucked into her collar asked, very quietly, whether kneeling again would get her daughter taken like the other children were taken. She learned it at the dead pump station, where the pipe-fitter who had whispered the six words to his crew the night before stood with his arms crossed and would not meet her eyes, because the foreman had watched the district die on a screen and called it a hoax, a poison the corporation was doing them the mercy of removing.

She learned it most of all from a girl named Lumen, thirteen, with a hacking cough and a jaw set like a trap, who found Vega in the smoke and said, "I want to do it. Teach me the words."

"Are you sure?" Vega asked. "The trucks are still out. The spray is still falling. What happens to the green, you feel it in your chest. And they're watching now. They quarantine districts. They take people."

"I know," Lumen said. "My sister got taken in the first burn. I've been waiting four years for something worth getting taken for." She knelt in the ash of a dead courtyard, where a single green stem pushed up through a crack in the concrete, stubborn and thin, and she touched it with both hands, and she breathed with it. The stem trembled, and under the pressure of her small fierce attention it began, slowly, to climb the crack.

Vega stood over her and felt the girl's song enter the chorus — thin, new, brave — and understood the second lesson, the one that hurt more than the first: leadership was not protecting the people who believed. It was asking them, again and again, to risk everything on a connection they could barely see, and trusting that the asking was worth it.

The quarantine came down like a lid. Helios declared the affected districts 'biological contamination zones,' the phrase repeated on every sealed channel until it meant nothing, which was the point, and the enforcement divisions ringed them with barriers and sensor arrays that could smell a green spore from a mile away. They sprayed in patterns now, methodical, grid by grid, and where the mist fell the green died, and Vega felt each death, and the chorus in her chest thinned and thinned.

But the strike was not centralized. That was its genius and its terror. It had never been a thing Vega or Sable could stop or break or lose, because it was a story, and a story does not live where you can find it. It lives in the telling.

The mother at the ration queue told her sister, and her sister told her husband, and the husband told a man who drove a dead frequency relay. The pipe-fitter who would not meet Vega's eyes went home and found a green shoot pushing up through the floor of his own cellar, and knelt in the dark where no one could see him, and breathed with it until his chest ached. The children of the districts carried the six words the way they had carried ration tokens, and when the enforcement trucks rolled past, they whispered them into drains and vents, into the soil of window boxes, into the ears of the green that waited under everything.

Each new bloom made the quarantine harder to sustain. Each new singer was a dead end the sensors could not follow, because you cannot quarantine a rumor. The barrier ring went up, and the story climbed over it in a hundred thousand mouths. The sensor arrays learned the smell of one strain of green, and the wild green — waking now, learning, spreading through every pipe and duct and forgotten mains the way water finds cracks — grew a thousand variations overnight, until the arrays began to scream at false positives, at nothing, at the memory of rain.

Inside the sealed Fold, in a white room where the air never changed, Silas Marlowe sat watching the maps of contamination spread like a slow green infection across the districts he had ordered quarantined, and for the first time in his careful, reasonable life, he panicked. Not visibly. Not loudly. He was a man who regretted having to speak. But he pressed the button for more spray, and more spray came, and the green kept coming, and he began to wonder, with the cold professionalism of a man watching his own machine fail, whether he was fighting a crop or a conviction.

It was not only the Fold's enemies who noticed. Somewhere in the vaulted maintenance levels of the arcology, a ventilation tech named Voss — a man who had never knelt, never heard the six words, never seen the green except in training holos — stopped at a junction box and sniffed the air coming off the recyclers, and thought: this is not what the air is supposed to smell like. It was stale. Flat. It had the dead, scrubbed taste of a thing filtered a hundred times, that had forgotten what it was filtering for. He checked the log. Nothing wrong. The system ran at perfect efficiency.

And yet, for the first time in his life, Voss opened the access hatch and let a breath of unfiltered duct air touch his face, and wondered, briefly, stupidly, what the world had smelled like before they had built the walls to keep it out.

He closed the hatch and told no one. But the thought stayed, the way a seed stays, and inside the Fold — where the sealed world had always smelled exactly as it should — more and more people began to notice that it didn't.

Vega knew none of this. She stood at the edge of the dead courtyard at dusk, Lumen's green stem still climbing the crack behind her, the spray trucks still cutting their grids through the smoke, and she felt the chorus thin again as another district's green went dark under the mist. The first seed on her wrist had gone dull with grief. She had asked a mother to risk her daughter. She had let a thirteen-year-old kneel in a quarantine zone. She had watched the green die in waves and felt every death, and she would do it again tomorrow, because the only thing worse than the cost was the silence that had come before it.

Sable came up out of the smoke, the dead radio in her hand, her one good eye scanning the barriers.

"They're saying we're finished," Vega said. "That the spray killed it. That it was a hoax."

"Let them say it," Sable said. She knelt, heavily, and put her scarred hand flat on the ash beside Lumen's stem. "A hoax doesn't grow."

And there, under her hand, thin as a rumor, a new thread of green pushed up out of the dead concrete and began, stubbornly, to climb toward the failing light — not because Vega had asked it to, not because anyone had commanded it, but because a story, once told, does not stop being told. It only changes tellers.

The sky above the quarantine ring shuddered green, just for a moment, and somewhere inside the sealed Fold a man who had never knelt was beginning to wonder why his world smelled so stale, and a panic was cracking, hairline by hairline, through the mask of a reasonable man.

chapters.name: The Botanical Garden
chapters.content:
The way in was a garden. That was the joke Vega could not stop turning over as she moved through the dark of the Fold's maintenance spine, and the joke had teeth, because the garden was real: the Helios central botanical garden, a glass dome the size of a city block suspended in the middle of the arcology like a lung in a ribcage — a sterile monument to a hundred years of pretending that control was the same as love.

It had taken her eleven days to get here, and it had taken Voss to bring her. The ventilation tech had found her by the one green thread running through the Fold's own ducts — the tamed, pacified network Helios had bred for its filters, singing its thin dumb song through every recycled breath. Vega felt it the moment she crossed the barrier and followed it up through the vaulted maintenance levels the way a drowning person follows light. There she found Voss at his junction box, his access hatch still open, smelling the world he had never been allowed to have.

"You're the one," he said when she stepped out of the duct shadows. "The one the broadcasts are about." He did not reach for an alarm. "I opened this hatch three days ago and I haven't been able to close it since. The air in here tastes like a thing that's been dead a long time and told it was alive."

"Then help me," Vega said, "and I'll show you what it tastes like when it's real."

He gave her the gardener's uniform, the clearance card, the schedule of the cameras that swept the dome in a loop for the Fold's citizens — the same cameras that had carried Marlowe's kind face into the world the morning her mother died. The plan was not hers or Sable's. It was the green's. She had knelt in the dead courtyard with the first seed dull on her wrist and asked it, truly asked, what it wanted of her now, and the answer came up through the ash like a pressure behind her eyes: go where they keep us caged and show them what a garden is.

The dome rose around her like a held breath. It was perfect — that was the terrible thing. Lawns clipped to velvet, flowerbeds in military rows, a single great tree at the center with its branches trained into a symmetry no wild thing had ever grown. The air was wet and warm and utterly sterile, and Vega, who had spent her life reading the thin green thread of buried life under the poisoned world, felt nothing here but a vast polite emptiness: a choir taught to hum, not to sing. This was what Helios called nature. A prisoner that had forgotten it was in a cage.

She knelt at the base of the great tree, in the exact center of the dome, under the sweep of the cameras. She put her bare hands flat on the manufactured soil, and she breathed with it.

The green heard her. It came up through the dome's false floor the way it had come up through the ash of the cistern, through every pipe and duct she had carried into the Fold on the soles of her boots, through the tamed filter network Voss had opened to her. The manicured lawn rippled. A vine slid out of the soil and wrapped itself around the great tree's trained branches, and the tree, freed of its symmetry, shuddered and began, tentatively, to grow crooked. Vega felt the whole chorus rise behind her eyes — the wild network and the tamed one meeting for the first time in a hundred years in the corporation's own showcase — and understood she was not alone in the air anymore, and never would be again.

The cameras found her. They had been built to find the center of the dome, and she had put herself there. On every screen in the Fold, on every sealed channel in every arc and board and city, the picture cut from the schedule to a girl in a gardener's uniform kneeling at the foot of a tree that was turning green in front of the world.

Marlowe came within minutes. Not the Marlowe of the broadcasts — the calm, kind, reasonable man who regretted having to speak. This one was moving fast, flanked by white uniforms, and Vega saw the thing she had hunted for since the night of the burn: the crack in the mask. His face was a man's face, tired and frightened, a man who had watched his machine fail for eleven days and had come to see the part that was failing.

The white uniforms raised weapons. Marlowe held up one hand, and they stopped.

"Vega Cardona," he said, reading a file he had memorized. "The carrier who got out of the burn. I've been looking for you a long time."

"You found me," she said. "You always knew where I was. I was in every breath you sold."

The cameras were live. She felt it the way she felt the green — the whole sealed world watching a girl kneel in a garden that had begun to riot around her, flowers opening out of season, the great tree leaning toward her like a listener.

"Turn the cameras off," Marlowe said, and nothing happened, because the room was a dome and the cameras were everywhere, and the men who ran them stood in front of screens showing a tree turning green and none of them moved.

"Here's the truth," Vega said, and her voice carried because she made it carry, the way Sable had taught her to make six words carry through smoke. "Your power was never yours. It was borrowed. A hundred years ago this world was a garden, and you took the gardener, bred it dumb and small, and sold the air it made back to the people it should have been breathing for free. You didn't build the sky. You murdered it and sold the corpse."

She held up her wrist, where the first seed lay dull but alive.

"But it's still here. It never stopped being here. It's in your filters, in your ducts, in the soil under this floor. It's been singing to you your whole life, and you bred it until it forgot the words." She pressed her hand to the soil. "So I brought it back to show you what you've been afraid of."

The green rose where she touched. A tendril — thin, bright, uncut, wild — pushed up out of the manufactured soil and climbed her wrist, twining with the dull seed, and the seed flared green and warm again, and Vega felt the whole chorus of the world rise in her chest and pour out of her open hand.

And then, deliberately, she turned her hand toward Marlowe. It was not an attack. There was no violence in it. The tendril simply extended — a green question, an offering, the same gesture the Verdant had made to her in the Undervault when it asked for a reason to believe. The cameras caught it. The world watched a thin green vine reach across the manufactured grass toward the most powerful man alive, and wait.

Marlowe looked at it. His face did not crack. It closed — the way a door closes gently, on purpose. "No," he said, to the tendril, to the cameras, to her. "I built this world. It doesn't offer me anything. I'm not in debt to a weed."

And he turned his back on the green and walked out of the dome, and the white uniforms followed, and Vega thought, for one terrible breath, that she had lost.

But the world had watched. That was the thing Marlowe had never understood, the thing Kael had known twenty years ago and said to her in a dead bus in the lamplight: "That's what the truth is for."

The cameras did not turn off. They stayed on the garden, on the tree leaning crooked and alive, on the green threading up the glass, and inside the Fold the screens played it on every channel, and the people who watched were the people whose air had always tasted stale, who had spent eleven days wondering why their world smelled so wrong.

Voss was first. Of course he was. He was already standing at his junction box, and when the broadcast came on he reached up, calmly, and opened every hatch in his section, and the unfiltered air came through, and he breathed it, and he wept.

Then the windows. One by one, across the hundred stories of the Fold, workers opened the sealed panes that were not meant to open. The alarms screamed and nobody cared. An arc-community in the upper tiers tore back their own filters, panel by panel, because the green was threading up the outside of the glass and they wanted to smell it. A woman in a white lab coat knelt on the floor of a genetics lab and put her hand on a potted plant bred for forty generations to be silent, and the plant, which had never been allowed to sing, sang for her.

The enclaves did not fall. Nothing was breached. No wall was stormed. The walls simply stopped mattering, because the people inside them had looked at the green reaching toward the man who owned their air, watched him say no, and understood, all at once, that they were allowed to say yes.

Vega stood in the middle of the garden with the vine wrapped around her wrist and felt the whole sealed world opening around her like a fist testing the idea of opening — the windows, the hatches, the filters coming down — and she thought of her mother, who had died for a jar of green milk and called it enough; of Mika, safe in the terminus hall; of Kael, in a cell somewhere, listening to sirens; of Sable, kneeling in ash and saying a hoax doesn't grow.

"Look," she said to the cameras, and her voice broke, and she let it. "Look what you were afraid of."

The tree at the center of the garden, free of its symmetry at last, put out one crooked, impossible branch toward the open sky, and the sky above the Fold — the real sky, shut out for a hundred years — shuddered green.

set.name: Vega Cardona
set.description: Eighteen-ish (still the seventeen-year-old of the story's opening, now hardened), orphaned, brother safe, the first seed and first voice of a worldwide movement. I'm not in debt to a weed' — and turned his back and walked out of the dome.
